video_title: Lawfare Daily: The President’s Hand in Russia’s Covert Action
transcript: This is the Lawfare Podcast. I'm Benjamin Wittes, editor-in-chief of Lawfare, along with Public Service Fellow Julia Gurley. We assess the 10-year covert operation that Russia conducted in 2016 to help Donald Trump. What rating does it deserve? Did it help Russia? Did it harm Russia? Did she do a little bit of both? How does it look against the backdrop of the most notable covert operations of all time? Congratulations on the 10th anniversary of the most successful covert operation in history, Julie. So, what do you think they give a secret operation for its 10th anniversary? So, should we view this as a birthday, that she is still growing and developing, and we are preparing her for a bar mitzvah, or should we view this as a decade-old event that we are celebrating? I think we should see this as an ongoing activity. Spoiler. Because it was never fully completed , at least in the sense that Russia's external influence operation, its covert operation to influence US policy, never ended. And this article, I hope, will make it clear that what we are seeing now in our midterm elections is just a continuation of something that really began during the Cold War, but which entered our consciousness as a country in a very tangible way 10 years ago. Yes, you mentioned the article, and I think we should clarify the terms we're using here. Julie, which article are you talking about? Thank you, Benjamin Wittes. We're talking about an article I wrote for Lawfare on the 10th anniversary of Russia's covert interference in our 2016 election called "The Unhidden Hand"—my way of labeling what we consider a covert operation, where the hand, when we're talking about the United States or Russia, should remain hidden as part of the operation itself. It could be conducted by the CIA, it could be conducted by the Russian GRU or the SVR. This is what intelligence agencies do, this is one of their main functions—covert operations. And America became the object of one of the most successful such operations in history about 10 years ago, the beginning of which fell on that time. Um, and I wanted to look at this not just because it was an anniversary, but because I wanted to look at it as a CIA officer who was evaluating the effectiveness of other domestic and foreign covert operations, and apply similar metrics that we would use at Langley if we were evaluating a Russian operation, and highlight a few key points. First, we evaluate success not only at the moment of the start of the operation, but over a period of time. We analyze whether it remained secret, whether it achieved its original goals, and what the consequences were for the initiating and sponsoring country, i.e. Russia. Okay, let's look at this more or less in order. But let's start by defining the scope of the operation, because when you're a CIA officer evaluating a covert CIA operation, you have a clear understanding of its scope, goals, and objectives. Here we have to construct it ourselves, right? We have to rely on how the operation itself was conducted, as well as how the Russians talked about it, to the extent that they acknowledged its existence . And also, given what we know from other sources about Russia's strategic goals towards the US and other countries, we can build a certain picture. But how would you describe the purpose of this operation , why it was needed, and what were its planned scope and means? They weren't involved in, you know, arming the mujahideen, for example, or, you know, publishing magazines in the United States. So what was this operation for and what did it consist of? Yes. Let's look at the situation globally, from Earth's orbit all the way down to ground level. So, first of all, classically there are three types of covert operations. You know, these are political influence operations, propaganda, political actions—that's exactly what these Russian efforts were. The Russians use the term "active measures" to describe this. Two other types that it wasn't: it could be sabotage targeting the country's defense-industrial base, or paramilitary action—that's what you mentioned, training insurgents, like the US did with the mujahideen in Afghanistan. This operation fits into the first classical category. This is an art in which the Soviet Union was a true pioneer in the world, and they continue their efforts to this day. This campaign was an attempt to achieve three main goals, which we can judge from what the CIA believed at the time. The 2017 Intelligence Community Assessment clearly identified three objectives based on information stolen by the Russians . The first was to harm the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton, whom the Russians viewed as an enemy. The second one was...Yes. Sorry. Success. Success on election night. Second. Next item on the to-do list. The second was to help elect Donald Trump. Donald Trump was elected. OK. Point two. We cross it out. It is worth pausing to say that it is impossible to scientifically prove that Russian aid was a decisive factor. It is worth noting, however, that in the three states where Donald Trump won— traditionally Democratic states—the difference between Trump and his opponent was a total of 78,000 votes. Just as we will never know whether Russia succeeded in helping him win, we will never know whether it was wrong. This is one of those... Right, but that's of course true when you take active steps to influence the political system and it moves in that direction; It is also impossible to say which Republican advertising campaign was effective under these circumstances. It is very difficult to determine what role external hidden components of the campaign may have played. But still, if you participate in covert operations and complete the first two items on the list, you can check them off—you're doing pretty well. Certainly, the operatives at the GRU and the Internet Research Agency were happy to take credit for this victory in their annual evaluations, I'm sure. This undoubtedly had some impact on our elections. And this is obviously an issue that was hotly contested, and the president, who received that kind of support, felt that it was somehow damaging to his legitimacy as president. I just wanted to point out that this is one of the unknown factors. And the third goal was, in fact, to delegitimize democracy in the United States or to undermine the faith of the people, the public, that their system is fair, legitimate, and works for them . Um, and in that sense, as we've seen over the past decade, it's also been an extraordinary success in terms of forcing the question of whether a foreign government elected our president instead of us. Part of this operation was to secure support for both the far left and the far right, amplifying them with the help of Russian bots and Russian social media. They are known to have convinced protesters from both sides to come to the same event and speak out against each other. So this effort to contrast the extremes of American society with the center—this is a classic Russian disinformation measure, and it was one of the main directions of their work. Good. And yet, we didn't really need 10 years to appreciate all of what you just described. All of this was essentially intelligence findings in 2017, and to the extent that , you know, Donald Trump said in the summer of 2016, "Russia, if you're listening," you know, please, no one denied that Russia did certain things in 2016 and tried to interfere in the election. So we don't need 10 years to look back and evaluate it if those are those three goals. You could...We did this back in the fall of 2016. Your statement is a bit broader, namely that the intervention was ongoing, and we now have 10 years of consequences to assess. I assume they relate more to this third question than the first two . Is this fair? That's fair. So one of the key messages of this piece is that while Russian interference did occur, every single investigation, including those conducted by the FBI under the direction of the president and special counsels, even those that were largely oppositional, like the John Durham investigation, no one has denied the basic fact of Russia's attempt to interfere in our elections. This has been proven repeatedly. No, I'm talking about how Russia's greater achievements occurred over the next 10 years after that. And these achievements, the main performer, the invisible hand right in front of us, almost too big to notice, is the efforts of the President of the United States. So, first it all starts with covering up the root cause , at least trying to convince his own political base that nothing happened , because he felt it threatened the legitimacy of his presidency. Then there were systematic efforts to delegitimize the investigators and the investigation itself, which included, uh, attempts to prosecute key individuals who were involved. And finally, uh, in this act, pending the re-election of the president. What we are witnessing now is a dismantling as it systematically goes through the very institutions that protected us from Russian interference, that announced it when it was happening, and dismantles those institutions even now, during our midterm elections, while the same actors on the other side, the Russians, are trying to influence the political process in the United States. And in this way, the president himself played a crucial role in giving Russia the maximum gains it has achieved since the beginning of its covert operation back in 2016. And what is... this brings us to the question you outlined at the beginning: what are your long-term consequences? Do you know if your long-term results are consistent with your short-term goals? You know, if you think about US support for the Mujahideen, yes, it really worked while the Soviet Union was in Afghanistan. But then, you know, later on, some of the mujahideen factions merged into, um, Taliban factions that became aligned with Al Qaeda, and boy, that's not...the long-term effect doesn't look as good as the short-term effect. In this case, it seems like things only get better and better the further you look into the future. And I think the question is, is there any, you know, I mean, first of all, what evidence is there that this activity is continuing? And secondly, how should we assess the long-term—not just the point-by-point consequences of 2016, but the long-term outcomes of the policy from the perspective of the Russian covert operation. Regarding the first question about evidence of its continuation. So we saw the US government constantly doing assessments in 2020, during the midterm elections in '18, in the elections in '20, in '22, and every two years in the US government you get the same assessments that were formed in 2017. And all of them, to the extent that they have been declassified and made public, show only a continuation of the same Russian influence operations that never succeeded in changing votes in terms of the mechanical counting of elections. But this continuation is evolving along with the different technologies that have emerged during this period, as we've gone from social networks like Facebook to Twitter under the name X and Elon Musk, and now we have the development of AI that creates deepfakes of celebrities supporting Democrats. Right now we see videos of Robert De Niro and Cher criticizing Democrats, even though they are both longtime supporters of Democratic candidates, and these videos are being shared in hotly contested states. Fake videos of key Democratic Senate candidates in Texas, and a new one in Maine today of candidates saying outrageous things—these are edited deepfakes that private cybersecurity companies have already traced to known Russian cybercriminals, continuing efforts we've been tracking since 2016. There is a real question now in the scientific literature, as well as in the corridors of power: when you evaluate a covert operation, at what point do you stop the countdown, because what began in the 16th is not a straight line to what is ongoing today. And you pointed out some classic examples of this related to support for the mujahideen . Do you blame this directly on the emergence of Al-Qaeda as a kind of " boomerang effect"? That's a good question, but obviously other things were happening in the interim, so we should be cautious in drawing conclusions. What I would point out is the consistent role of the same characters in this particular covert operation: whether it's the same actors in Russia, the GRU and the alleged private Russian cybercriminals, or whether it's the consistent efforts of the same person, the beneficiary of the initial effort—Donald Trump, who is using this and also trying to keep other things out of it. So I would point out this contrast that we are currently observing. He is taking active steps to promote a false foreign conspiracy theory—this idea that China is interfering in our elections— while making no effort to combat the real foreign attempt to influence the election in his favor by promoting candidates who would support his positions and his party, and attacking those who would not. At the same time, he has taken active steps to dismantle the institutions that exposed the interference in 2016 and that would now protect us from further Russian influence operations directed against his political opponents. So I think that this is how the secret operation that began in the 16th can be fairly assessed up to this day. OK. Let me make a point about which, in my opinion, a reasonable person might be skeptical. You are confusing Donald Trump's behavior with the behavior of the most secret operation, with the activities of the most secret operation. And our skeptic might say: “Well, okay , Julia Curley is either identifying Donald Trump with Russian intelligence here, that is, implying that he is some kind of agent , or she is simply being devious and saying that everything Donald Trump does, since the goal of the covert operation was to elect him , should be considered a consequence of that operation.” Um, and I probably want you to open this up a little bit and say: Are we looking at Donald Trump here as a product of a covert operation, as a beneficiary of it, as a partial effect? And why don't we just view him as, you know, an American politician who has some sort of overlap of interests with a Russian covert operation, like getting himself elected, or smearing his political enemies? He hates certain people and organizations that the Russians also want to discredit. And, by the way, he loves Vladimir Putin as much as he loves other dictators. So, you know, this is what we call "parallel play" in toddlers. You know, they both do their thing in the same room, and boy, do they seem to like the same toys. I think many of these comments are valid . But where I would object is that I was assessing the situation here from the perspective of Russia , or at least the sponsor, because that's how in measures of the effectiveness of covert operations we look at how the sponsor won both then and later. And from that perspective, it was a bet, an investment that continued to pay dividends, rooted in the original stock. But the fact is that from the Russian perspective, the details of the case don't matter whether he is actually a Russian agent . The joke in the coffee line at Langley, and I'm pretty sure this isn't classified information, was this: if the president isn't an agent of a foreign power, then he's chosen the wrong vocation. Because no one could tell them apart, as he seemed to be acting in accordance with Russian goals in the world. Was it to smear US allies, divide our friends and unite our enemies, was it to refuse to help Ukraine in its time of need on the eve of war and now during war in a way that benefits Russia, or was it to lift Russian sanctions simply on the eve of an election that the Russians are actively interfering in to sway the results in its favor, right now. So in a way, it's even better for the Russians if it's not actually objectively an asset that's somehow managed from afar. More often than not, when you look at other examples of individuals in the broader data set who received support from foreign intelligence or a foreign state, they have to be supported over time. As a rule, they are weak. They do not have the same support base and organic foundation that the president has. And in fact, the best practice in intelligence when planning effective covert operations is to work with what's already there, amplify it, promote it as a legitimate or organic element in society, and provide the resources for success in a way that simply aligns with your goals. And in that sense, I think the Russian investment has probably paid off much more than anyone could have expected. So I'm not trying to say that the Russians were some kind of "Svengali" who could see into the future about all the president's actions , but from their perspective, from the sponsor's perspective, these events turned out incredibly well, and that leads to assessments like those of former director Michael Hayden that this was the most successful covert operation in world history. Okay, but that also creates a certain methodological problem in retrospective assessment, because it raises the question: assuming that, first, we don't know whether this action had a helping effect, in the sense of providing meaningful assistance to his cause. Crucial help. Help. We don't know if he actually believed in all these things and wanted to do them anyway. Could it be that all these things that look like positive outcomes from a sponsor's perspective are actually just lucky guesses, and, you know, you bet on the right horse, but that doesn't mean you made the horse win the race, right ? You get paid because you bet money on it , but you didn't make, well, let's say, a horse run faster than another one, and if you think about a covert operation, it's not like betting on Kalshi, is it ? This is, in fact, an attempt to influence the outcome . So my question is: is there a way to know , by evaluating this covert operation, what the relationship is between causation and correlation? Undoubtedly, this series of events—and when you read the article, it's very striking—the events that took place almost exactly coincide, and we'll touch on a few exceptions, with Russian interests. But is there a way to know whether this means the covert operation was successful and not just a good bet on the future? You hit the very heart of the methodological problem that I think is unavoidable when evaluating covert operations: it's a question of causality, coincidence, or what actually caused the outcome, and you're right. What-what? And to that I might add: if we are going to draw global conclusions about covert operations, we are talking about covert activities for which our data set is limited, including the US. So we're saying that this is one of the most successful covert operations in history, while the dataset I was able to use is unclassified materials collected by a CIA historian, which end in 2011 . So who knows, maybe there are other key examples to compare. Yes, because we have been doing so well since 2001. We are doing very well. So this, this is a very difficult question. I mean, from that data set, we deduced what seem to be the best practices of covert operations that this operation followed, and, you know, whether it's using what's there and building on it, or the conclusion that for these kinds of political actions, almost all successful cases occur when the supported party, the beneficiary, welcomes the support, accepts it, builds on it and doesn't deny it or try not to hide it after the fact. The reason for this, and why this operation has paid such dividends, is that most covert actions lose their effectiveness over time, because when they are exposed, the target country restores its defenses, because even the supported actor does not want the permanent stigma of illegitimacy that comes with such foreign support. So they often, even as beneficiaries, turn away from it; they condemn it; They say, "No, no , no, it's been me all this time." And then they restore protection so that the benefits to the foreign country disappear, and , in fact, this can lead to significant backlash, especially in a democratic system. In this case, we have the opposite, and whether this is coincidence or causality , we may never know for sure. But what we know for sure is that Russia's biggest gains from this came after election day. They have manifested themselves in active efforts by the supported side to dismantle defenses , divide American society, and harm America's ability to intervene in world affairs in a way that is clearly beneficial to Russia. Do we want to draw a straight line to each other, that's, you know, one of the main challenges in assessing covert actions, I'm just saying that as a question. As a matter of what the profession does , we would put these matches together, and you know, the more matches the better, and if it all works out in the sponsor's favor, we would rate it as a successful undercover operation. OK. Let's talk about some of the disadvantages from a Russian perspective. The Russian economy is a disaster. They are partly a reaction to US sanctions , which are partly a reaction to this. Although most of them concern Ukraine . So how do you understand the flip side of this ? And I suppose there's another downside overall, which is that Russia didn't just do this in the United States. She did it all over Europe. She did it wherever she could. They seem to enjoy such influence operations, and they are building up both far-right and nationalist movements, as well as the far-left. I mean that both the Left and the AfD are pro-Russian to some extent. Both the far left and the far right in France are pro-Russian or at least sympathetic to Russia. And all of this has generated real anger at Russia, related to the situation in Ukraine, but not limited to it, in almost all Western countries. So are they losing by winning here, or is this an example of a covert operation that is successful enough and has such a lasting effect that you're willing to tolerate, well, let's say , a Biden administration at the center of it all? This is again a problem of where exactly you draw the line for evaluation. If we were doing this analysis in the middle of the Biden administration, say, a few months after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and before Donald Trump returned to the White House and wreaked all this havoc, dismantling the institutions that had kept Russia from interfering further, you might see it as the same case of a massive failure , a blowback that inspired the United States to oppose Russia and perhaps to support Ukraine more than it might otherwise have done. So in that parallel universe, this would be considered a failure with significant negative consequences. And we really see this as a key problem of covert interference in democratic elections, and that's why the United States, at least in the modern era, has historically avoided it because of the risk of backlash and reputational damage to the United States. The difference, of course, is that Russia, even though it was exposed from day one, seemed to suffer no real domestic consequences for interfering in the affairs of another country, simply because of the nature of the Russian regime. They did not suffer. And thanks to the actions of the supported party, which is really the crucial element in this case, they were able to continue to enjoy these advantages and then neutralize some of the things that could be called backlash, such as the support of Ukraine by the United States under this administration. But this is certainly a difficult question. If in two years we see the return of a democratic president with a burning desire to punish Russia for its past crimes, we could find ourselves in a similar situation. I mean, you can really imagine a situation where for 10 years they live only on the remnants of resources, and Russia goes from a fairly favorable geopolitical position in 2015-2016 —when Germany was in a very friendly and accommodating position, when it controlled 10% of Ukraine's territory in the format of a frozen conflict, and although relations with the West, the Obama administration, were difficult—its international position was by no means catastrophic . Now imagine that in two years the US will have an administration—and not even necessarily a democratic one, but simply with a traditional consensus in foreign policy—and suddenly the West unites. Assuming that Germany is not run by the AfD and Le Pen is not leading France, this creates a terrible geostrategic position for the Russians. So I think it's best to understand it this way: the first 10 years of this plan worked well, except for the fact that the Russians themselves ruined everything by invading Ukraine , turning a large part of the world against them , and this certainly contributed to their downfall and reaching "bottom." On the other hand, whether they can continue in the same spirit is a big question. This gave them time to strengthen their international positions, but they didn't actually do it. So I think we should take this as a demonstration of the limits of what even the most successful covert operations can actually achieve. I think that is absolutely correct. I mean, I'm making a kind of assessment of the effectiveness of the GRU here , and they shouldn't be held responsible for the invasion of Ukraine, which took place later on the orders of the president. And, trying to be as objective as possible, I will say that this intervention is not the "Rosetta Stone" to explain everything. This is not an assessment of Russian policy in general . No, there were many other counter-actions that Russia took in the following decade that caused serious damage to the Russian economy and its people, most notably the invasion of Ukraine. Good. So, if you were giving a lecture at Langley on this topic, and a young cadet raised her hand and asked, Ms. Curley, what are the lessons of this for us? Not as for us, as the recipient of covert actions, you know, but as for a nation that itself is conducting covert operations, and we are not. What should we learn from this? Should we actively interfere in the internal affairs of many countries? And should we conduct covert campaigns in Greenland? What, you know, what lesson of success should we take from this for our own covert operations? I think in some ways it validated some of the best practices that we teach officers, but in other ways it's probably a unique case. This is likely something unique to these circumstances, and the Russian regime itself, being different, at least for now, than a democratic country, would suffer consequences for interfering in the internal political affairs of another democratic state. At least traditionally that is the case. I would say that learning from this is that the covert operation in this case was successful in part because it was narrowly focused and had very specific goals. Two of the three could be measured on election night. It was relatively inexpensive. Some covert actions achieve success by being a bit more expensive, but most successful ones are actually not that expensive , and if they are expensive, then you are probably using the wrong tool. You should probably do something overt that uses the resources of other United States institutions, such as the military, to achieve your goal. This was part of a larger policy, so the covert efforts were coordinated with the overt actions of the Russians—whether it was weakening U.S. power, trying to force the U.S. to focus on domestic problems, or dividing us and our allies, it was all coordinated . They were not trying to perform some insidious miracle that would contradict the Russians' public statements. And, most importantly, they exploited the target's existing weaknesses rather than trying to create new ones out of thin air. They accurately diagnosed the subject, Donald Trump, as a divisive figure with a real support base in the United States. Maybe they predicted that once he came to power, he would be able to be manipulated, maybe because of his worldview—his vision of the world as such, where, you know, like a mafia boss who divides the world between three families, and where everything is built on deals, which coincides quite well with the Russian worldview. So choose your goals carefully and build on existing successes. Um, I would take a step back, though, and talk to the class, and maybe I would turn on the greatest covert operations movie of all time, at least the part from Charlie Wilson's War where Gast Avrakots, one of the main ideologues of this, is asked to toast the success of the operation. And he replies: "We'll see." Because he has seen this before and knows that over time, success can fade, and the consequences can be very real. And the film mentions the rise of Al- Qaeda, which, in fact, was the case. One can argue about direct cause and effect, but it's a lesson in humility about what we can truly achieve with this tool, which is best used as a scalpel, not a hammer. And as for the United States, I think we, as a country, are not very well-suited to using this tool to interfere in the political systems of other states. We have a pretty poor track record of maintaining positive results over a long period of time. I think it was quite successful at the beginning of the Cold War . Italy. Once or twice. But a strong argument can be made, if you look at US interventions in Iran, that interference in Iran's internal processes helped lay the groundwork for the emergence of the IRGC. Um, I don't, I don't, and the Iranian revolutionary regime. Of course, many other events were happening at the time , but Iranians vividly remember the interventions in their country and the attempts to keep the Shah on the throne. So you should be extremely careful when using this tool. What about the defensive aspect? You conclude the article with two lessons for us as a country that has become the target of this Russian covert operation. I want to read them out and then ask you to elaborate on each one. Ten years later, Russia's 2016 operation teaches us two lessons. First, foreign intervention has the most lasting effect when the beneficiary has every incentive to hide the sponsor's hand. Second, protection against further intervention must be built in such a way that no leader who benefits from foreign influence can dismantle it. So I flip a coin, press start, and… start talking. You know, as with many things, when we think about how to secure the presidency from Trump, I'll start with the caveat that it may not be possible to completely secure the presidency from the president himself. But there are probably things we could do to increase resistance so that, as I've discussed here, the problem of the winner's veto can be mitigated. So if the person receiving the aid has an incentive to hide it and perhaps even allow additional aid from a foreign entity to come in to help them, we have a real problem . What we do to counteract this is have strong institutions that can resist the president. And if they are within the executive branch, perhaps they can appeal to Congress through accountability mechanisms that would allow the inherent checks and balances of the US system to kick in in time to take action, assuming there is the political will, which in this case was not there, to intervene. That's why in the article I talked about doing more to enshrine in law, rather than in decrees, key institutions that would protect against this type of dynamic. So if the current president disbanded the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force , it should be ensured that this is enshrined in law, funded by Congress, and has regular reporting requirements to the appropriate committees on Capitol Hill, so that it is clear whether the president is trying to disband it. The same can be said about the ODNI Foreign Influence Task Force. The same can be said about CISA. Enshrining these institutions, which have a legislative basis in some, but not all, cases, I believe is a reasonable response on the part of Congress. Reporting requirements, in my opinion, are critical to requiring the intelligence community to provide assessments of foreign interference or influence that is occurring before an election, but are not currently required to make this data public. We now know, based on statements by Senator Warner and Representative Himes of the House and Senate Intelligence Committees, respectively, that these classified reports were provided. Analyzing the situation and the press coverage of their words, it sounds as if they are saying: yes, influence operations are ongoing, but there are no reports we can rely on that actual ballots have been altered. Requiring a public assessment before the election and then a retrospective public assessment after it could be another way to create such barriers so that it is not so easy for the president, who controls the executive branch, to silence these voices that the winner-takes-all veto gives him . We will stop there. Julia Gurley, the article is called "The Unhidden Hand." She was published in Lawfare a few days ago, on October 22, about how Russia's biggest dividends from 2016 came from the president she helped win. Thank you for joining us today . Thank you, Ben.
